extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / Royal Society members / 17th‑century scientists and replicators
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting procedural, observational, and structural standards from a Philosophical Transactions issue (experiments, botanical anatomy, observational astronomy, medical/surgical reports) to evaluate or replicate early-modern scientific reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix cold phosphorus with oil of vitriol to produce fiery balls (Expt. II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure as reported: take between 10 and 20 grains of solid phosphorus, melt it in just enough water to cover (about a drachm); after it is actually cold, pour it into 2 oz. of oil of vitriol; shake the mixture — it first heated and then threw up such fiery balls that adhered to the sides of the glass and continued to burn for some time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact quantities given; observe resulting luminous/combustive 'balls' adhering to glass. No separate safety note here, but see other experiments' cautions about open vessels and ignition risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce flame by adding oil of turpentine to the foregoing mixture (Expt. III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add a small quantity of oil of turpentine to the phosphorus+acid mixture; without shaking the vessel, the mixture takes fire and burns very furiously. Succeeds with oil of petroleum and 'de lateribus'; sallad oil and spirit of wine did not flame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shake after adding the turpentine; select an appropriately inflammable oil (oil of turpentine, petroleum, etc.). Perform in an open vessel with free access of air (see separate guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform inflammatory mixtures in an open vessel (general procedural safety)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This experiment ought to be made in an open vessel, where the air has free access.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open vessel both for experimental success (air access) and safety (vent fumes, reduce risk of pressure build-up or concealed ignition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test claimed spontaneous accension in dark conditions and avoid optical fallacies (Expt. IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: To refute Borrichius's claim that turpentine is inflamed by aquafortis when exposed to sunlight, repeat the experiment in a dark room — red fumes seen in sunlight can represent flame by reflected beams but may be a fallacy; in the dark no spark or light is produced though violent fermentation and smoke occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform in dark to distinguish true light from sunlight-illuminated fumes; keep candles at a distance because the fume will ignite at an actual flame and may set the liquors burning (safety caution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for successful inflammation of oil of turpentine by nitrous acid (replication notes / footnote)
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote caution: Borrichius's assertion is not disproved — successful inflammation may require well‑rectified oil of turpentine and concentrated, smoking nitrous acid; the manner of mixing (pouring acid upon oil at different intervals rather than all at once) may be requisite for success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rectified oil, concentrated 'smoking' nitrous acid, add acid gradually (not all at once). The effect may be greatly promoted by adding a small quantity of strong vitriolic acid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ebullition and great heat from red spirit of nitre + rectified spirit of wine (Expt. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: On 1 oz of spirit of nitre, pour 2 or 3 drachms (gradually) of the highest rectified spirit of wine — the heat and ebullition are exceedingly great and performed in an instant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use red spirit of nitre and a very high rectified spirit of wine. Order matters: pour the spirit of nitre (heavier liquor) into the glass first, then add the spirit of wine after; inverting the order prevents ebullition. Pour gradually rather than all at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold produced without ebullition via sal ammoniac solution (Expt. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissolve a quarter of a pound of sal ammoniac in about a pint of water; the solution is 'so very cold to the touch' that a thermometer was not required to convince the experimenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation by touch is reported; the author tentatively relates this to physiological phenomena (hysterical paroxysms) but notes that such application is 'by no means satisfactory to philosophers or physicians' (caveat on overinterpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold produced by violent ebullition to resemble ague fits (Expt. VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting a volatile salt of human blood into acids (vinegar, verjuice, wood-sorrel, orange, lemon, or stronger acids) produces notable ebullition with a manifest descent of the thermometer (cold). The higher (stronger) the acid, the greater the ebullition and the cold produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reach near-freezing effects use very strong vinegar 'dephlegmed by freezing' or spirit of Venus/verdigrise; expect the mixture to swell and require deep vessels (won't be contained in shallow vessels). Note the author warns of unexpected phenomena (expansion with cooling) and contrasts with cases (oil of vitriol + water) that produce heat without expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five general heads of inquiry for a complete history of plants (Anatomy of Plants: project rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea prefixed gives materials and methods under five general heads of inquiry: 1. Those things of external consideration about plants (figures, etc.); 2. Their compounding parts (vessels, etc.); 3. Their liquors and other contents; 4. Their principles (salts, etc.); 5. Their aliment (water and other means of growth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five heads constitute the foundational rubric for composing a 'philosophical history of plants' aiming at discovering the reason of vegetation and the virtues of plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter structure for plant anatomy: anatomy then uses; seed treated twice
rubrics_metrics.description: Anatomy is divided into chapters: in every chapter the anatomy of the part is first given, then the uses are subjoined. The work begins with the seed and proceeds to root, trunk, branch, leaf, flower, fruit, and lastly the seed to be sown again. There are two chapters for the seed: the first shows the manner of its growth; the last shows the manner of its generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize each chapter with description/observation first and practical/functional uses after; treat seed with separate chapters for growth and generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start botanical observations with the naked eye before using microscopes
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first book, all the observations, except one or two, are made with the naked eye — 'that a proof might first be given, how far it is possible for us to go without the help of glasses,' since many lack microscopes and the patience to manage them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish what can be observed unaided before invoking microscopes; then employ microscopes for finer anatomy (roots, vessels, fibres, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content expectations per botanical book (roots, trunks, leaves/flowers/fruits/seeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Book II: anatomy of roots (naked eye + microscope), motions and properties of roots, anatomy of skin/bark/wood/pith, sap-vessels, air vessels/lungs, bladders, fibres, parenchymous parts, and vegetation of roots. Book III: anatomy of trunks and branches, motion/course of sap and air, structure, generation of liquors, figuration and mechanical uses. Book IV: leaves (protections, folds, surface features, apertures, texture, formation), flowers (three general parts and timing of formation), fruits (descriptions and uses), seeds (figures, numbers, motions, coverings, vitellum, foetus parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete anatomical history should treat structure, function, development/formation timing, and practical uses for each organ; include both descriptive and mechanistic remarks (motions, courses of fluids, textures, and generation of internal liquors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set of lectures/topics to accompany anatomical history (project syllabus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following lectures/essays are proposed to accompany the anatomy: I. Of the nature, causes, and power of mixture; II. Experiments on the luctation arising from mixture of several menstruums with bodies (specimen of natural history of materia medica); III. Essay on proportions of lixivial salt in plants; IV. Discourse concerning essential and marine (muriatic) salts of plants; V. Discourse on the colours of plants; VI. Discourse on diversities and causes of tastes chiefly in plants; VII. Experiments on the solution of salts in water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topical lectures constitute an extended research agenda and methodological rubric for a 'philosophical history' of plants; they indicate experimental directions (mixture, lixiviation, salts, colours, tastes, solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational criteria and signs to record in earthquake reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported indicators for earthquakes: seasonality (most common in Spring and Autumn), preceding rainy weather followed by calm and frost, abundance of vapours and nitre exhalations below ground, noticeable stench in well water, presence of 'ignes fatui' a few days before, barometer readings (height of quicksilver), calmness of air, and tremulous/vibrating ground motion often accompanied by a hollow murmuring sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate motion types (pulses/succussions vs. tremulous vibrating motions); record extent/area of effect and auditory phenomena; compare with other recorded earthquakes for scale and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for timing and observing eclipses/ingresses of Jupiter's satellites (astronomical observation guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eclipses/ingresses are calculated from tables; timings of ingresses (especially of the first satellite) are typically accurate to within about 5 minutes; these events are a good expedient for determining longitude. Observations are feasible with a telescope of 12 feet, or if needed 8 feet; note that telescopes made with two convex glasses invert the object so ingresses/emersions may appear on the opposite side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sufficiently long focal-length telescopes (12 ft preferred) for accuracy; be aware of instrument inversion when interpreting apparent positions; supply tables and publish predicted times sufficiently early for observers to use them for longitude determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording occultations: precise timing, micrometer use, and catalogue comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When observing occultations of fixed stars by the Moon, record exact times (by watch) for beginning and end of occultation, note altitudes, and measure positions with a micrometer; compare observed star positions with catalogues (and update catalogue positions when necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed time logs, repeated altitude measurements, and note if a star is absent from earlier catalogues (add to new catalogue with coordinates and latitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical protocol for excision of the caecum in a bitch and postoperative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Surgical steps as reported: open abdomen on right side in regio iliaca, pass knife through musculus obliquus ascendens and beside musculus rectus; locate and separate caecum from ileum by cutting membrane binding them; ligature the artery to the caecum; make three or four 'prick-seams' through sides at the distal end to stop passage of faeces; cut off caecum about 1/8 inch from stitches; sew new lips entering needle on the inside and passing through the outer membrane so the lips touch edgewise to promote union; sew wounds, tie the bitch away, provide milk post-op.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor recovery: small intake of milk next morning, progressive recovery over weeks, observe fatness and breeding performance; perform subsequent autopsy to confirm healing and absence of compensatory deficit. The reported case showed good recovery and no evident functional loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postoperative evaluation criterion for anatomical indispensability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether removal of an organ causes functional deficit by observing the animal over months (behaviour, appetite, fatness, ability to reproduce) and by post-mortem examination (position of omentum, healing of wound, evidence of compensation). In the reported case no alteration 'that might reasonably be imputed to the loss of the caecum' was observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prolonged observation and autopsy to evaluate organ necessity; absence of observable change is taken as evidence the organ's use is 'a desideratum' (i.e., not yet established).
